verified_ref: Nitishataka 89 in GRETIL (Chaukhamba ed., 1.89), Telang/Joglekar 89, Kale 89 and Wortham 89 (under 'The Power of Fate'). Our label 'Nitishatakam 90' matches none of them.
translation_note: Matches Joglekar and Kale. Both read karma here as deeds of past lives and buddhi as one's inclination or impulse to act ('proclivity', Joglekar). Wortham 1886 reads the first line quite differently (discernment as the fruit of former deeds), so English renderings vary.
context: Sits in the run of verses on fate (daiva). Just before it, Indra loses a battle despite Brihaspati, the thunderbolt and Vishnu on his side (88); just after, a bald man who seeks shade under a palm is killed by a falling fruit (90). Between these fables of helplessness, this short verse concedes karma's hold and then insists on careful conduct. The verses praising action begin a few stanzas later.

key_terms.sense: the result one meets depends on (past) deeds
even one's inclination of mind follows those deeds
even so: the turn of the verse

core_teaching: What happens to us, and even the way our minds lean, is shaped by earlier deeds; that is no excuse. The wise still act only after careful deliberation.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Warns that the first half could suggest a person is wholly at the mercy of past deeds, but says thinkers hold one can shape one's future by present deeds; compares Gita 6.5 (raise yourself by yourself).

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the fruit as the pleasure or pain that deeds bring and sees an allusion to the traditional divisions of karma; renders the close as acting only after mature consideration.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes karma as acts done in a past life and links the verse to the following stanzas on merit stored from former births; otherwise grammatical notes.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to hold two truths together: you did not choose your starting conditions or even all your habits of mind, but you still owe the next decision your full attention.
misreadings: Not fatalism: 'tathāpi' (even so) turns the verse toward responsibility
Not a claim that people deserve what happens to them
cautions: The first line can sound like blaming a person's misfortune on their past deeds; do not apply it to someone's illness, loss or abuse
speaks_to: feeling boxed in by circumstances or old patterns
after a setback, when tempted to stop thinking things through
not_for: someone grieving or harmed, for whom 'karma' can sound like blame
a reader already paralysed by overthinking
research_note: Our id/label number is one higher than every edition checked (GRETIL/Chaukhamba, Telang via Joglekar, Kale, Wortham all agree on the lower number).

verified_ref: Nitishataka 92 in GRETIL (1.92), Telang/Joglekar 92, Kale 92, Wortham 92; the same stanza recurs in the Vairagyashataka in Telang's and Wortham's editions (Vairagya 110). Our '93' matches none of them.
attribution_note: Found in both the Niti and Vairagya collections (Telang, Wortham).
translation_note: Close to Kale ('if it makes the man short-lived, woe to its folly'). Joglekar reports one commentator who reads it as: creating such a person is itself folly if he is to be broken soon after. 'Perish in a moment' fairly renders tat-kṣaṇa-bhaṅgi.
context: Among the verses on the power of fate. Just before, the poet sees sun and moon seized by eclipse, elephants and snakes in bonds and wise men in poverty, and concludes fate is mighty (91). Just after, no one can wipe away what fate has written on the forehead (93). This verse turns the theme into a cry against a Creator who wastes his finest work.

key_terms.sense: the unwisdom of the Creator / fate

core_teaching: A lament, not a lesson: fate creates a person of rare goodness, an ornament to the world, and then breaks them at once; the poet calls this folly.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains puruṣa-ratna as a jewel of a man endowed with every virtue; records a commentator who places the folly in creating such a person at all if he must soon be destroyed; notes the verse recurs in the Vairagyashataka.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as fate first producing an ornament of the earth and then making him short-lived, and exclaims at fate's folly; takes tāvat as emphatic, 'indeed creates'.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Prefers 'the jewel man' over 'a jewel-like man' and reads the opening as 'does indeed create, but then...'.

practical_reading: Used in grief writing to give permission to protest an early death instead of explaining it away; the poet does not console, he names the unfairness.
misreadings: Not a theological claim that God is foolish; it is a poet's lament inside a section on fate
Not a consolation; it gives no reason for the loss
cautions: Directly about the sudden death of an outstanding person; raw for fresh grief, especially an untimely death
Blaming the Creator may jar for devout readers
speaks_to: grief over someone taken too soon
anger at the unfairness of a loss
feeling the world wasted someone good
not_for: a reader who needs reassurance that loss has meaning
someone facing their own serious diagnosis, who may read it as a verdict
research_note: Our id/label number is one higher than every edition checked (GRETIL/Chaukhamba, Telang via Joglekar, Kale, Wortham all agree on the lower number). Our_note's claim that 'the tradition lets the protest stand' is not stated in the sources read; it is a fair editorial reading.

verified_ref: Nitishataka 94 in GRETIL (1.94), Telang/Joglekar 94, Kale 94, Wortham 94 (first verse under 'The Praise of Action'). Our '95' matches none of them.
translation_note: Matches Kale and Joglekar. Both read the 'fixed actions' as deeds already done (Joglekar: in a former state), so karma here means deeds and their consequences, not only present effort. Our line 'Bow to what you do' leans toward present effort; acceptable but slightly modernising.
context: Opens the praise of action in Wortham's arrangement and answers the run of verses on fate just before it. The next verse bows to the karma that made Brahma toil like a potter, sent Vishnu through ten incarnations, made Shiva beg with a skull and keeps the sun circling. The argument climbs from gods to fate to deeds.

key_terms.sense: giver only of the fruit fixed by each deed

core_teaching: Gods answer to fate, and fate only delivers what deeds have earned, so the real power lies in deeds; the poet bows to karma, over which even fate has no say.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Notes the gods are finite, their rule ending with the aeon; fate has no arbitrary power and dispenses fruit strictly by men's actions; the poet distinguishes vidhi from karman; the figure is a climax.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Says Bhartrihari makes karma the thing on which even fate's course depends; translates the fruit as that of settled deeds done in a former state.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Places it at the head of 'The Praise of Action' and ends with adoration paid to works over which fate has no power.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to move attention from luck and divine favour to conduct: what you do is the one lever every other power must respect.
misreadings: Not irreverence toward the gods; it is a rhetorical ladder
Not a promise that present effort always wins; in the commentators' reading karma includes past deeds whose fruit is already fixed
cautions: Can feed self-blame if read as 'whatever happened to you, you caused'
speaks_to: feeling dependent on luck or other people's favour
wanting to take ownership of one's life
not_for: someone suffering a loss they did not cause
a reader wrestling with guilt
research_note: Our id/label number is one higher than every edition checked (GRETIL/Chaukhamba, Telang via Joglekar, Kale, Wortham all agree on the lower number).

verified_ref: Nitishataka 99 in GRETIL (1.99), Telang/Joglekar 99, Kale 99, Wortham 99. Our '100' matches none of them.
translation_note: Joglekar and Kale both gloss āvipatteḥ as 'until death', vipāka as ripening or consequence, and śalya as a splinter or dart lodged in the body. Our line softens 'until death' to 'for years', which is fair. Wortham 1886 reads the foresight as aimed at release from rebirth.
context: In the run praising action: after verses on merit from former lives protecting a person anywhere (97) and on good conduct turning poison to nectar (98), this verse turns practical. The next verse compares wasting a human birth to cooking sesame husks in a jewelled pot over sandalwood.

key_terms.sense: a result that burns the heart like a lodged splinter

core_teaching: Before any undertaking, good or bad, weigh where it will lead; the results of rash acts lodge like a barb and keep burning for the rest of one's life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses rabhasa as rashness, āvipatteḥ as up to the time of death, śalya as a foreign body causing great pain, and vipāka as ripening, hence result.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Same reading: the result must be considered beforehand; the issue of acts done in hot haste is, till death, like a dart in the vitals; the figure is simile.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Takes the point of looking to the end as freedom from births in another state, a more otherworldly reading than the Bombay editors give.

practical_reading: Quoted as a pause-before-you-act rule: a hasty word or decision can leave a regret that outlasts the moment by decades.
misreadings: Not advice to avoid all risk or decision
Not a claim that every regret is permanent or unforgivable
cautions: For someone already tormented by a past rash act, 'burns until death' can deepen shame
speaks_to: about to send an angry message or make an impulsive decision
big financial, career or relationship choices
not_for: someone stuck in regret over a past mistake
anxious over-planners who need encouragement to act
research_note: Our id/label number is one higher than every edition checked (GRETIL/Chaukhamba, Telang via Joglekar, Kale, Wortham all agree on the lower number).

verified_ref: Nitishataka 101 in GRETIL (1.101), Telang/Joglekar 101, Kale 101, Wortham 101. Our '102' matches none of them.
translation_note: Matches Joglekar and Kale. Our Sanskrit has śatrūn (plural) where GRETIL reads śatruṃ; no change in sense. Kale stresses that the listed feats are ways of seeking wealth (diving for pearls, Meru's gold, battle, trade), so the verse is about gain that is not destined.
context: In the praise-of-action run, right after the image of wasting a human birth (100) and before the verse that, for a person with great past merit, a wild forest becomes a city (102). Despite the heading, these verses keep conceding what earlier deeds have already fixed.

key_terms.sense: by the force of past deeds

core_teaching: However heroic or skilled the effort, what is not destined will not happen and what is destined will not be undone; the reason given is the force of past deeds.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Draws the moral that one may attempt the hardest and most dangerous things to bring about what is fated not to happen, or to avoid what is fated, and will fail.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Disputes half of Telang's moral: the verse says nothing about avoiding the fated; it says wealth sought by pearl-diving, Meru's gold, war or trade will not come if it is not destined.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'all sciences and arts' as the traditional fourteen sciences and sixty-four arts, and construes 'by the force of karma' with 'never happens'.

practical_reading: Teachers pair it with the verses on effort: do everything you can, then loosen your grip on the result, because outcomes depend on more than you.
misreadings: Not a reason not to try; nearby verses praise industry (Niti 86)
Not a claim that every detail of life is pre-written
cautions: Read alone it is fatalistic; it can crush someone who tried everything and failed, or sound dismissive after a loss
Pair it with an effort verse, as our misuse note says
speaks_to: after giving one's best and still not getting the result (exam, job, fertility treatment, business)
letting go of obsessive control over outcomes
not_for: someone deciding whether to try at all
fresh bereavement, where 'it was meant to be' can feel cruel
research_note: Our id/label number is one higher than every edition checked (GRETIL/Chaukhamba, Telang via Joglekar, Kale, Wortham all agree on the lower number).

verified_ref: Nitishataka 103 in GRETIL (1.103), Telang/Joglekar 103, Kale 103, Wortham 103. Our '104' matches none of them.
attribution_note: In Wortham's edition this verse opens the 'Supplementary ślokas' that follow 'The Praise of Action'; our setting ('from the section on action') is not supported by a heading in the editions checked.
translation_note: 'Samaya-cyuti' has two senses in Joglekar and Kale: letting the right moment slip, or breaking an engagement; Wortham read 'failure in one's duty'. 'Nipuṇatā kā dharma-tattve ratiḥ' is 'perfection: devotion to one's religious principles' in Kale; our 'skill: love for the heart of dharma' is fine. 'Anuvratā' is a devoted (faithful) wife; ours says 'faithful wife', correct.
context: A question-and-answer verse (praśnottara) among the closing stanzas of the Niti collection, after the runs on fate and action. Riddle catechisms like this were a common teaching form.

key_terms.sense: letting the moment slip / breaking an engagement
one who has mastered the senses
not having to live away from home
power whose fruit is being obeyed

core_teaching: A catechism of values: real gain is good company, real loss is a missed moment, real courage is self-mastery, real wealth is learning.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Gives both senses of samaya-cyuti (missing the right moment; breaking an engagement) and glosses kingship as the capacity to command and enforce obedience.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Translates nipuṇatā as being devoted to one's religious principles, anuvratā as a wife devoted to her husband, and happiness as not going on a journey.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains samaya-cyuti as letting slip an opportunity and kingship as the power whose fruit is command; quotes the Sanskrit commentary on the rest.

practical_reading: Teachers lift single lines: self-mastery as courage, learning as wealth, and the real cost of missed timing.
misreadings: 'Happiness is not living abroad' is a period sentiment about exile and homesickness, not a judgment on migrants
The 'beloved = faithful wife' line reflects its time; do not present it as teaching on marriage roles
cautions: Contains gendered and dated definitions; quote selectively and say so
Can sting for emigrants or people working far from home
speaks_to: someone who keeps letting opportunities pass
not_for: readers living abroad or homesick (the apravāsa line)
conversations about marriage or gender roles
research_note: Our id/label number is one higher than every edition checked (GRETIL/Chaukhamba, Telang via Joglekar, Kale, Wortham all agree on the lower number).

verified_ref: GRETIL 1.104; Telang/Joglekar 105, Kale 105, Wortham 105. Our '105' matches Telang, Kale and Wortham (which have an extra verse before it), not GRETIL.
attribution_note: Like the previous verse, Wortham places it among the 'Supplementary ślokas', not under 'The Praise of Action'.
translation_note: Matches Joglekar and Kale (poor only in harsh words, rich in kind ones, content with their own wives, averse to slander). 'Sva-dāra-parituṣṭa' is literally 'content with their own wives'; our 'spouses' is a gender-neutral modernisation. Wortham 1886 mistranslates the compound as poor men whose words count for nothing.
context: A short āryā verse among the closing Niti stanzas, describing the rare good person; the neighbouring verses praise steadiness that does not bend in misfortune.

key_terms.sense: poor in unpleasant words, i.e. never speaking harshly

core_teaching: Only here and there is the world adorned by people who never speak harshly, always speak kindly, are faithful in marriage and do not speak ill of others.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains the paradox: 'poor' in disagreeable language means not given to harsh words, 'rich' in agreeable language means habitually kind; the world is only sparsely adorned by such people.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Gives the same reading and glosses parivāda as censure of others.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders the first compound as poor men whose words are of no account, inverting the sense; a warning that old translations can mislead on this verse.

practical_reading: A reminder that kind speech and refusing to gossip are rare and beautiful; useful for reflecting on how we talk about people who are not in the room.
misreadings: Not praise of material poverty; 'poor' and 'rich' refer to speech
cautions: The fidelity clause names 'their own wives' in the original; our translation modernises it
not_for: someone hurting from a partner's infidelity, where the fidelity clause may sting

verified_ref: GRETIL 1.106; Telang/Joglekar 107, Kale 107, Wortham 107. Our '107' matches Telang, Kale and Wortham, not GRETIL.
translation_note: Matches Joglekar and Kale. Editors differ on the verb for the glance-arrows (a reading meaning 'cut/wound' as in ours, or one meaning 'pierce'); the sense is the same. GRETIL has a typo 'kipa' for 'kopa'.
context: Among the closing Niti verses on the steady person (dhīra). Just before, a constant person's courage is like a flame that points upward even when the torch is held down (106); just after, one hero lights up the whole earth like the sun.

key_terms.sense: the heat of the fire of anger

core_teaching: The truly steady person is not wounded by desire, not burned by anger and not dragged by greed; such a person has conquered more than any king.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Translates: the firm man whose mind is not pierced by glances, consumed by anger, or ensnared by greed for many objects prevails in the three worlds; discusses the variant verbs for the arrows.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Prefers the idea of piercing for the glance-arrows and reads the three clauses as parallel negations describing the courageous man.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Defends his chosen verb because piercing suits arrows and 'burning' already goes with the fire of anger.

practical_reading: Used to redefine strength as inner mastery: anger and greed are named as enemies, and not being ruled by them is the real victory.
misreadings: Not a claim that women are dangers; the glance-as-arrow is a stock image for desire
Not a demand to feel nothing; it is about not being cut, burned or dragged
cautions: The first image casts women's glances as weapons; our line rightly omits it
not_for: someone ashamed of their feelings or desires, who may hear condemnation

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 3 in GRETIL (Chaukhamba ed., 3.3) and in Madhavananda 1916 (Nirnaya Sagar order); Telang/Joglekar and Wortham number it 4.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar. 'Dhmātā' is smelted (ores fired in a furnace). Madhavananda explains the nights at the cremation ground as rites for summoning supernatural help to get riches; Joglekar links them to the pursuit of powers through incantation.
context: One of the opening verses that censure craving (tṛṣṇā-dūṣaṇa). Verse 2 lists hard travel, servility and eating at others' doors; this verse lists treasure-hunting, alchemy, sea voyages, courting kings and graveyard rites; verse 4 adds smiling through tears before the rich. Each ends by speaking directly to Desire.

key_terms.sense: worship with mantras, here to gain power or wealth
Craving, have your fill now (be satisfied)

core_teaching: A catalogue of everything done for gain, even occult shortcuts, ends with nothing gained; the poet tells his own craving to be content now and let him go.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Footnotes the cremation-ground nights as part of secret rites by which people invoked supernatural agencies to obtain riches.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Notes that fortunes are still wrecked by alchemy, that power through incantation was a common chase, and that the cremation ground on full-moon or eclipse nights was the usual place for it.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes the opening as digging because one suspects treasure is there, and weighs Ramarshi's glosses on the smelting phrase, finding one strained.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: In his free rendering the worthless cowrie becomes a cowrie 'of blessedness', giving the futility a spiritual edge.

practical_reading: Speaks to the exhaustion of chasing money through scheme after scheme (speculation, quick-rich plans, endless side ventures) and to the moment of finally saying 'enough' to the wanting itself.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of honest work or ambition as such
Not a claim that effort never pays
cautions: Mentions cremation-ground rites; harmless but may need a gloss
speaks_to: burnout after years of chasing money
losses from risky schemes or speculation
not_for: someone struggling to meet basic needs, for whom 'enough craving' can sound contemptuous
a young person who needs encouragement to work

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 6 in GRETIL (3.6) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 13.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar, who both supply the hidden reasons: we bore wrongs because we could not avenge them, and left home comforts because we could not have them or went abroad after wealth. GRETIL reads 'nityamita-prāṇaiḥ'; ours 'niyamita-prāṇaiḥ' (with breath controlled); same sense.
context: In the opening censure of craving. It follows verses on servile flattery and on risking one's fragile life for gain (4-5) and comes just before the famous 'we did not enjoy pleasures, they enjoyed us' (7). The poet sees that his worldly life copied the outward acts of ascetics with none of their inner reasons.

key_terms.sense: endured, but not out of forgiveness
with breath held, as in meditation

core_teaching: The worldly person ends up doing what sages do (enduring, giving up comfort, bearing hardship, fixing the mind) but for the wrong reasons, and so misses every fruit those acts bring the sages.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Adds the hidden motives in brackets: forgiving from inability to right one's wrongs, giving up home comforts as an exile in quest of riches.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Sums up: neither the pardoning nor the leaving of home involved self-denial; the pain endured chasing earthly things equalled an ascetic's, yet produced no merit.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Gives the same sense of the first line, prefers a reading of the second for syntactic uniformity, and finds the Sanskrit commentary on this verse involved and unclear.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to ask why we do what we do: the same act (patience, sacrifice, long hours, discipline) can build us or empty us depending on its motive.
misreadings: Not saying forgiveness or sacrifice are worthless; it is about motive
cautions: Can feel accusatory to someone who sacrificed out of necessity, e.g. migrant workers or carers
not_for: someone who endured abuse, who may hear 'you didn't really forgive'
exhausted caregivers

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 7 in GRETIL (3.7) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 12.
translation_note: Madhavananda notes the double senses that English cannot keep: bhukta = enjoyed / eaten up; tapta = (austerity) performed / scorched; jīrṇa = worn down / aged. Ours captures all four turns.
context: The climax of the opening censure of craving: right after the verse on doing ascetics' deeds for the wrong reasons (6) and before 'wrinkles on the face, only craving stays young' (8). Vivekananda joined verses 5 to 8 into one passage in his free translation.

key_terms.sense: pleasures were not enjoyed (eaten); we were
austerity was not performed; we were burned
time did not pass; we did
craving did not grow old; we did

core_teaching: We think we consume pleasures, practise discipline and spend time; in truth pleasures consumed us, worry scorched us, we passed while time stayed, and we aged while craving stayed young.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains each pair as an ironic pun: time is not gone because it is ever-present and infinite, but we are gone because death draws near; the effect cannot be kept in translation.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'we were enjoyed' as becoming the objects of enjoyment (by death) and 'we were heated' as by worldly anxieties instead of austerities.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely within a combined passage: we did not enjoy, enjoyments enjoyed us; we did no penance, penances burnt us.

practical_reading: Widely quoted on consumerism and ageing: the habit of wanting outlives the body and the years spent feeding it.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all joy; the target is craving (tṛṣṇā)
Not despair about growing old
cautions: Blunt about ageing and lost time; may sting for readers carrying heavy regrets
speaks_to: feeling used up by work or consumption
not_for: someone in depression who already feels life is wasted
terminally ill readers, without careful framing

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 8 in GRETIL (3.8) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 14.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar. GRETIL spells the first word 'balibhir' for 'valībhir' (wrinkles).
context: A short verse right after 'craving did not age, we did' (7), making the same point through the ageing body. Verse 9 then pictures an old man on a stick still startled by death.
core_teaching: The body visibly ages in every part, but craving alone keeps getting younger.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates it plainly: the face attacked by wrinkles, the head painted white, the limbs enfeebled, desire alone rejuvenating.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses each word and compares a Panchatantra stanza (V.38) making the same point that desire does not age.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Cross-refers to the 'bhogā na bhuktāḥ' verse and to stanza 15 of the Mohamudgara (Bhaja Govindam) as a parallel.

practical_reading: A mirror for later life: the body slows, but the mind's wanting (status, possessions, control) may not; noticing that gap is a place to begin.
misreadings: Not mockery of old people
Not saying older people should stop enjoying life
cautions: Describes bodily ageing plainly; can feel unkind to someone distressed about ageing or illness

habits that persist despite changed circumstances

key_terms.sense: one's peers have gone to heaven (died)
startled at the approach of death

core_teaching: Even when every reason to cling to life has fallen away, the body still recoils from death; the poet calls this clinging foolish.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Adds that the friends went to heaven before being overtaken by old age, allows that the blindness may be cataract, and calls the body's alarm a silliness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses mūḍha as impudent or shameless and timira as an eye disease; offers two senses for the lost respect: pride of manhood or esteem among men.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Prefers 'respect among men' and cites Tawney's comparison with verses of Maecenas on clinging to life even when crippled.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to name the instinctive fear of death that survives every argument, as a starting point for inner work rather than for shame.
misreadings: Not contempt for the elderly or for fear of death
Not encouragement to neglect one's health
cautions: Mentions the death of friends, frailty, failing sight and fear of dying; heavy for the elderly, the bereaved or the ill
speaks_to: noticing that fear of death persists despite age
not_for: recent bereavement

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 10 in GRETIL (3.10) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 45.
translation_note: Madhavananda renders āśā as Hope; Joglekar and Wortham as Desire. GRETIL's 'viśuddham alaso' is a corruption of 'viśuddha-manaso'.
context: Our data places it at the close of the opening censure of craving. After the portraits of the ageing body (8-9), the poet gives an extended allegory: expectant craving is a river full of hazards that only pure-minded yogis cross.

key_terms.sense: hope as anxious expectation, craving for what is to come

core_teaching: Expectant craving is a dangerous river: fed by wishes, churned by longing, full of passions, doubts and delusion, it uproots fortitude; only yogis of pure mind reach the far shore and rejoice.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Reads vitarka as scheming thoughts of greed, the birds on the river, and dhairya-druma as the trees of patience and fortitude that it destroys.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Renders āśā as Desire: passions are the crocodiles, doubts the birds, infatuation the eddies, anxiety the steep banks; happy the pure-hearted ascetics who have crossed.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: His free version makes the yogis blissful because, with pure minds, they never crossed this river at all.

practical_reading: Used to map anxiety: each feature of the river (wishes, worry, doubt, attachment) names a mental habit to notice; helpful for people caught in rumination about outcomes.
misreadings: Not against hope in the sense of courage or faith; āśā here is grasping expectation
cautions: Our gloss 'a river called Hope' can mislead a reader in despair; make clear it means anxious expectation
speaks_to: chasing a goal that keeps moving
not_for: someone in depression or despair who needs hope in the ordinary sense
readers in crisis

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 12 in GRETIL (3.12) and in the Madhavananda/Nirnaya Sagar order (Arunachala reproduction); Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 16.
translation_note: Matches Joglekar and the Madhavananda-style rendering on the Arunachala page: objects that tear themselves away cause great pain; given up voluntarily they bring endless peace.
context: In the section on the futility of trying to give up sense objects (viṣaya-parityāga-viḍambana). Just before, the poet finds even merit earned for heavenly pleasures frightening (11); just after, he marvels that the wise can drop wealth they actually enjoy while he cannot drop pleasures he only imagines (13).
core_teaching: Every pleasure and possession will leave us anyway; the only choice is whether we let go freely, which brings lasting peace, or have it torn away, which brings anguish.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Distinguishes two kinds of separation from pleasures, being left and renouncing; the peace that comes from having given them up is the difference; compares Gita 2.71.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes the stress on voluntary separation in the last line as the key, and compares the Gita's passage from 2.70 onward on the one who is not moved by desires.

commentaries.who: Madhavananda-style translation reproduced by Arunachala Ashrama
commentaries.gist: Adds that renouncing them oneself leads to the bliss of self-possession, while their tearing away greatly afflicts the mind.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to possessions, status, youth and habits: practise letting go before life takes them, so that loss when it comes is less of a wound.
misreadings: About things and pleasures, not advice to leave people before they leave you
Not a reason to refuse enjoyment; the point is the grip
cautions: Read near a bereavement, 'let go before it is taken' can sound like blaming the mourner for grieving
speaks_to: downsizing, retirement, ageing out of a role
fear of losing what one has
not_for: fresh grief over a person
someone who has just lost a job or home involuntarily
research_note: The OCR of Madhavananda 1916 is illegible at this verse; I used the matching rendering on the Arunachala Ashrama page, which reproduces Madhavananda-style translations without naming the translator.

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 19 in GRETIL (3.19) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 92.
translation_note: 'Vadhū' is read as 'wife' by Madhavananda and Joglekar; our 'a woman' is looser. The Sanskrit does say meat (māṃsādi-kalitam); Joglekar softens it to vegetables and condiments, Madhavananda keeps meat.
context: In the section on the futility of giving up sense objects: after the moth and the fish who do not know their danger (18), and before the man with mansions, sons, wealth and a loving wife who thinks the world permanent (20).

key_terms.sense: mistakes it for happiness, sees it upside down

core_teaching: What we call pleasure is mostly relief: drinking when thirsty, eating when hungry, embracing when desire burns. People mistake the cure of a disease for happiness itself.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says the point is that worldly happiness is a temporary remedy for the diseases of worldly life; once that is seen, one stops chasing it and seeks lasting peace in renunciation.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the last line as mistaking the mere cure of pain for pleasure itself, and notes Tawney compares a passage in Plato's Republic.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses viparyasyati as thinking wrongly, misunderstanding; translates the meal as rice with vegetables and condiments.

practical_reading: A tool for noticing that much 'pleasure' is just the ending of discomfort; useful for examining cravings like snacking, scrolling or shopping that relieve an itch rather than satisfy.
misreadings: Not saying eating, drinking or marital love are sinful
Not a call to deny the body its needs
cautions: Mentions meat and sexual desire; our line rightly keeps only the thirst image for general readers
not_for: someone with an eating disorder (food as 'disease' framing)
a reader in physical hardship or hunger

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 21 in GRETIL (3.21) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 8.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar. Telang adds that the sense is: a man of strong mind would not beg at all were it not for seeing his family so; it is the family that constrains him.
context: In the section censuring begging and servility (yācñā-dainya-dūṣaṇa). The next verses call the belly the root of all humiliation (22) and say a proud man would sooner wander a forest or beg in a holy city than plead among his equals (23).

key_terms.sense: the wife, mistress of the house
fear that the request will be refused

core_teaching: Self-respect would never let a man beg for his own sake; only the sight of his hungry family drives him to ask, with a choking voice, for help.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as no self-respecting man saying 'give me' for his own petty stomach, in a voice faltering for fear of refusal, if he did not see his wife and children suffering.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: States the sense plainly: a strong-minded man would not go about begging but for the state of his family; it is they who compel him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains the broken, choked syllables and notes a commentator's analysis of the compound; translates 'his accursed stomach'.

practical_reading: Speaks to the humiliation of asking for money, loans or favours for one's family, and honours the love that swallows pride.
misreadings: Not contempt for people who ask for help
Not a teaching that providing is only a man's role
cautions: Vivid picture of hungry crying children and a wife in rags; painful for readers in poverty or debt
Gendered household roles
speaks_to: a parent swallowing pride to ask for help
job loss, debt, borrowing from relatives
not_for: someone in acute financial crisis looking for hope (the verse offers none)
readers sensitive to gender roles
research_note: Our line ('For his hungry family, he swallows his pride') is warmer than the verse, which belongs to a section mocking the misery of begging; fair, but note the shift.

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 29 in GRETIL (3.29) and Madhavananda 1916; in Telang/Joglekar and Wortham it is not in the Vairagya at all but Niti 'Miscellaneous' stanza 16.
attribution_note: Doubtful authorship: Telang notes that the Sharngadhara Paddhati (p. 220, Banaras ed.) ascribes this stanza to Vidyapati, and he placed it among the miscellaneous (non-core) Niti stanzas. Safer wording: 'from the Vairagyashataka attributed to Bhartrihari'.
translation_note: First half is fine. The second half is garbled: the Sanskrit asks for whose sake the Creator made Meru, that great store of riches whose golden glory stays within itself, and ends 'Meru does not please me' (Madhavananda, Wortham, Joglekar). Ours ('for whom did fate make wealth, and what kind of place is it?') loses that Meru is the subject.
context: In our data's section on begging and servility (the Nirnaya Sagar order). Madhavananda's nearby verses praise forest food and the begging bowl over flattering the rich (26-30).

key_terms.sense: whose golden glory ends in itself
Meru does not appeal to me

core_teaching: Contented people already have unbroken joy and greedy people are never satisfied, so a mountain of gold helps no one; the poet does not want it.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains that Meru, the fabled gold mountain, serves no one: the contented are happy without it and the greedy are never satisfied; its gold glorifies only itself, so the poet will not covet it.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reports that the Sharngadhara Paddhati ascribes the stanza to Vidyapati; discusses how the closing question should be construed.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Translates: for whose sake was Meru, so full of wealth, created, since its golden splendour is confined to itself; finds part of the last sentence superfluous.

practical_reading: Used to question hoarding: wealth that sits unused helps neither the content (who do not need it) nor the greedy (who are never filled).
misreadings: Not a condemnation of earning; the target is greed and hoarded wealth
cautions: Low risk; mild reproach of the greedy
not_for: someone in real poverty, for whom 'wealth helps no one' may ring false
research_note: Translation needs a fix (see translation_note). Our verified_with correctly says it is not in the Wortham/Telang Vairagya; it is in their Niti miscellany.

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 31 in GRETIL (3.31) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 35. Vivekananda translated it (Complete Works vol. 9, verse 31).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar. key_terms.sense: in enjoyment, the fear of disease
in high birth, the fear of a fall
in honour, the fear of humiliation
dispassion alone is free of fear

core_teaching: Every good thing we hold (pleasure, family, wealth, honour, strength, beauty, learning, virtue, the body) carries its own fear of loss; only dispassion is without fear.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates each pair plainly and ends that all things of this world pertaining to man are attended with fear; renunciation alone stands for fearlessness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Discusses the 'silence' versus 'honour' readings, finding reticence a virtue that does not belong in this list; renders the close as asceticism alone free from danger.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Notes the 'silence' reading breaks the stanza's symmetry, so 'honour' is better: where there is a high sense of one's greatness there is danger of misery.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely as a litany ending: all in this life is fraught with fear; renunciation alone is fearless.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to show that anxiety is the shadow of attachment: every role and asset we cling to brings a matching fear, so loosening the grip loosens the fear.
misreadings: Dispassion is not giving up on life or people; it is holding things without clutching
Not a claim that anyone's fear is baseless
cautions: Mentions disease, old age and death in one breath; may feed health anxiety if read alone
speaks_to: anxiety about losing status, money, looks or health
high achievers who feel constantly threatened
not_for: someone in acute grief or fear, who may hear 'you should not have been attached'
a reader with health anxiety, without framing

key_terms.sense: disasters as if through open doors

core_teaching: Health is uprooted by countless ills, fortune lets disasters in after it, and death swallows everything born; nothing fate has made is stable.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains the grammar of 'makes its own' (complete subjection) and quotes Telang: what indeed has unbridled destiny created well-constituted?

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: around the root of health are a thousand worms of danger and disease; where is the Providence that made anything that did not die?

practical_reading: Used to puncture the illusion of permanence in health and prosperity, as a prompt to hold them gratefully and lightly.
misreadings: Not a reason to neglect health or prudence
Not cynicism about good fortune as such
cautions: Bleak and death-focused; can deepen despair or health anxiety
speaks_to: sudden illness or reversal after a good period
reflecting on the fragility of success
not_for: a reader newly diagnosed or bereaved
someone depressed or anxious about health

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 35 in GRETIL (3.35) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 54.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda (water on the edge of a wind-tossed lotus leaf). Joglekar's text reads abhra (cloud) for abja (lotus): life like water in scattered clouds. Joglekar ties the closing call to yoga to Patanjali's samādhi and the courage needed to overcome obstacles.
context: In the section on the instability of enjoyments, between the call to wise teachers to strive since the world is unsubstantial (34) and the verse that life is a wave and even embraces end (36).
core_teaching: Pleasures flash like lightning, life is as fragile as a drop on a wind-tossed lotus leaf, youth's longings do not last; knowing this, the wise should turn quickly to yoga.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Renders life as insecure as a drop on the edge of a lotus leaf dispersed by wind, and asks the wise to fix their minds firmly in yoga, easily reached through patience and equanimity.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Reads life as water in a small bank of clouds scattered by wind; explains that reaching samādhi needs strong courage against obstacles listed by Patanjali; discusses the compound.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders pleasure as lightning in a canopy of cloud and life as fleeting clouds, the cloud reading Joglekar also follows.

practical_reading: Used as an urgent nudge to start a meditation or spiritual practice now rather than 'later, when life settles'.
misreadings: Not saying pleasure is evil; it is fleeting
Not a demand to abandon family or work
cautions: Moderate; reminder of mortality
speaks_to: young adults noticing how fast years go
after a near miss or health scare
not_for: someone grieving a sudden death, where 'life is fragile' can feel like a lecture

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 36 in GRETIL (3.36) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 82. Vivekananda translated it (verse 36).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda, Joglekar and Vivekananda. 'Priyābhiḥ' is feminine plural (beloved women, in Madhavananda 'our beloveds'); our 'loved ones' is gender-neutral, which is fine for a general reader.

key_terms.sense: as fleeting as a passing thought
the ocean of fear that is worldly existence

core_teaching: Life, youth, wealth, pleasures and even the embrace of loved ones are brief; fix the mind on Brahman to cross the ocean of worldly fear.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains the 'fear' of the world as the dread of finding oneself bound by an afflicted world with no way out; attachment to Brahman is the crossing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely, saying our most beloved one is only for a moment, and urging the reader to give the heart to Brahman to cross this ocean.

practical_reading: Used to invite reflection on what lasts when every relationship and possession is temporary; in a devotional reading, to anchor the heart in the divine.
misreadings: Not telling anyone to stop loving family
Not saying human love is worthless; it is saying it is not permanent
cautions: 'Even the embrace of loved ones does not last' is very painful for the newly bereaved or separated

speaks_to: after the end of a relationship, once the rawness has passed
not_for: fresh grief or divorce
new parents or lovers in a joyful season, where it can feel like a cold shower

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 38 in GRETIL (3.38) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 109. Vivekananda translated it (verse 38).
translation_note: Translation fine. The line ('still we spend it hurting each other') narrows 'ahitam ācarati': Joglekar reads it as people injuring themselves or leading an evil life, Madhavananda and Vivekananda as doing wicked deeds; our_note's 'what is not for one's good' is closest.

key_terms.sense: does what is harmful, not for one's good

core_teaching: With old age crouching, illness attacking and life leaking away, it is a wonder that people still spend their time doing what harms them.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates the close as how wonderful that man still goes on doing wicked deeds.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses ahitam ācaranti as doing injury to themselves or leading an evil life; parisravati as dribbling, passing away; the jar is cracked.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: old age watches, roaring like a tigress; life flows out like water from a broken jar; curious that men still do evil.

practical_reading: Used as a wake-up call to stop spending limited time on grudges, self-destructive habits and petty harm.
misreadings: Not fear-mongering about ageing; the point is the use of time
cautions: Predatory image of old age; can frighten older or ill readers
speaks_to: someone stuck in a feud or grudge
a reminder to use time well
not_for: elderly or ill readers already afraid

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 41 in GRETIL (3.41) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 37. Vivekananda translated it (verse 41).

key_terms.sense: passed into the path of memory

core_teaching: A whole brilliant world (city, king, court, poets, beauties, princes, bards) now survives only as memory; the poet bows to Time, by whose power it all passed.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Glosses Kāla as time or the principle of change, and has the whole scene fleeting away along the way of memory.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Compares Niti 34; likens 'gone into memory' to the English phrase 'a matter of history'; notes the Sharngadhara Paddhati quotes a related stanza right after it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Reads the pronoun 'that' throughout as 'that well-known, familiar', giving continuity of remembered grandeur; translates 'homage to father Time'.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely as a roll-call of beautiful cities, mighty monarchs and moon-faced women all swept from memory, with salutation to Time.

practical_reading: Used for reflection when an era of life ends (a workplace, a home, a generation): honouring what was, without bitterness, and bowing to change.
misreadings: Not nihilism; it is an elegy that ends in a bow
cautions: Gentle; suitable for loss of a place or era
speaks_to: the end of an era: a closed business, a sold family home, a changed hometown
not_for: very fresh loss of a person, where 'only memory' may feel too stark

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 42 in GRETIL (3.42) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 39.
