key_terms.sense: house; also a square on the dice-board
the world as a game board
living beings as the game pieces

core_teaching: Households fill and empty, from many to one, from one to many, and finally to none: Time plays a game on the world's board, throwing night and day as dice, with living beings as its pieces.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'home' as also a square of a checkerboard; expert Kāla moves the pieces, casting the two dice of day and night, until none remain at the end of the game.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes the two players as the male and female personifications of destruction, Shiva and Parvati, whose dice game is famous in the Puranas; notes the house/square pun.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Follows Telang: Kāla and Kālī play dice on the earth as a dice-board, living beings as pieces tossed night and day.

practical_reading: A way to see family change across generations (weddings, births, deaths, children moving away) as one long game no one controls.
misreadings: Not saying life is random or meaningless
cautions: Depicts households emptying and death as a game; can feel callous to the bereaved
speaks_to: a family home after elders have died
not_for: fresh bereavement
anyone feeling powerless or used by fate

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 43 in GRETIL (3.43) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 7. Vivekananda translated it (verse 43).
attribution_note: Telang notes the stanza also occurs in the Śāntiśataka (Kāvyasaṅgraha p. 319), so it circulated outside Bhartrihari's collections too.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda, Joglekar and Vivekananda. 'Trāsa' is fear or alarm; Joglekar renders it 'disgust'.
context: In the section on Time, after Time's dice game (42) and before the verse on people running the same daily course without shame at being fooled by repetition (44).

key_terms.sense: by the sun's coming and going

core_teaching: Each day shortens life, yet busy with work we never notice; seeing birth, age, trouble and death all around, we feel no alarm, as if drunk on heedlessness.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates the end as the world gone mad from drinking the stupefying wine of delusion.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Allows that 'time is not felt' can be construed with the busy affairs; glosses the wine as made of delusion.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Notes Tawney compares a stanza of the Palatine Anthology, and that the verse also occurs in the Śāntiśataka.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: crushed by many works we do not feel time fly; seeing birth, age, danger and death, we are not afraid.

practical_reading: Used to challenge busyness: a full calendar can hide the fact that days, and with them life, are passing.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of work; it is about heedless work
cautions: Mild; mentions death
speaks_to: feeling years have vanished in routine
not_for: someone who cannot slow down because of financial necessity (may feel like blame)

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 47 in GRETIL (3.47) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 48.
translation_note: Matches Joglekar (who keeps the damsels not embraced even in a dream) and Madhavananda (who glosses the crow image as passing all one's time greedy for maintenance from others).
context: Third of three stanzas (45-47) in the section on Time where the poet speaks as a man whose life has achieved nothing: no merit, no learning, no glory, no love, no service to parents. The next verse turns to parents and childhood friends long gone (48).
core_teaching: Looking back, the speaker finds he has gained neither learning nor wealth, not truly cared for his parents, not known love; his time has gone like a crow's, scrounging for scraps from others.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says stanzas 45-47 strike an anomalous note: the poet plays a man whose life was a failure, to show the vanity of a householder's aims; the poet cares more for drama than psychological precision.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses śuśrūṣā as attendance or service and the crow image as yearning for food meant for others; compares the third line of stanza 11.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders it with 'reverence towards our elders' not paid, generalising beyond parents.

practical_reading: Used for an honest life-audit: naming what was neglected (learning, family, love) as a spur to change while there is time.
misreadings: Not saying the reader's life is wasted
Per Madhavananda, a dramatic persona, not a model of how a seeker should think
cautions: Regret about not caring for parents can trigger guilt, especially after a parent's death
Mentions missed romantic love
speaks_to: someone resolving to reconnect with parents while they live
not_for: someone whose parents recently died
readers prone to depression or harsh self-judgement

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 48 in GRETIL (3.48) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 38.
translation_note: Close to Joglekar. The first line literally says those who bore us have long been familiar (Madhavananda: on intimate footing with Eternity, i.e. long dead); 'gone into memory' belongs to the second line. Our translation merges them slightly; acceptable.
context: In the section on Time, after the failed-life stanzas (45-47) and before the arithmetic of a hundred-year life (49).

key_terms.sense: long since familiar (with eternity), long dead

core_teaching: Our parents are long gone and those we grew up with are now memories; we ourselves, closer to falling each day, are like trees on a crumbling sandy riverbank.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the first line as parents now on intimate footing with Eternity, long dead; in old age we approach our fall day by day like trees on a sandy bank.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Translates: those from whom we were born have long since left us, those we grew up with are mere recollection, our fall comes nearer daily.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Discusses Ramarshi's gloss of the first word as 'familiar with Time' and finds it unsupported by anything in the verse except the section heading.

practical_reading: Speaks to the moment one becomes the oldest generation: honouring those gone and accepting one's own place on the bank.
misreadings: Not morbid: it is about seeing one's place in time
cautions: About the death of parents and peers and one's own nearing death; strong grief trigger
speaks_to: becoming the elder of the family
not_for: fresh bereavement on Day 1 of a grief plan
young readers or anyone with death anxiety

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 49 in GRETIL (3.49) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 107. Vivekananda translated it (verse 49).
translation_note: Matches Joglekar (half in night; half of the rest in childhood and old age; the remaining quarter in illness, separation and servitude). Joglekar discusses whether 'aparam' means 'the other' or 'in addition'. Vivekananda's free version divides the years differently.
context: In the section on Time, after the trees on the crumbling riverbank (48) and before the actor who exits behind Death's curtain (50).

key_terms.sense: a life measured at a hundred years
restless as a ripple on water

core_teaching: Do the arithmetic of a hundred-year life: half goes in sleep, much in childhood and old age, and the rest in illness, separation and serving others; where is happiness in so restless a life?

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Works through the arithmetic: the remaining middle portion is about twenty-five years, full of troubles, illness and separation, spent in servitude; cites Telang in support of the simpler reading.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Ends with life more uncertain than ripples on the surface of water.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely as 'where is happiness in this life?', with the hundred years parcelled out among sleep, decrepitude, childhood and serving others.

practical_reading: Our_note calls it deliberately bleak. Teachers use it to make time feel finite, a prompt to protect the hours that are truly one's own.
misreadings: Not a claim that life has no joy; it is rhetorical arithmetic meant to shock
cautions: Deliberately bleak; can deepen depression
Mentions illness and separation
speaks_to: feeling time is eaten by work and obligations
not_for: anyone depressed or hopeless
caregivers or people with chronic illness, for whom 'the rest goes in sickness and service' may feel like a sentence
research_note: Madhavananda 1916 OCR is damaged for most of this verse; only the closing image was legible.

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 50 in GRETIL (3.50) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 112. Vivekananda translated it (verse 50).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda, Joglekar and Vivekananda.
context: Our data places it at the close of the section on Time; it gathers the section's images into one: life as a play of quick costume changes ending in exit.

key_terms.sense: a youth in love with pleasure

core_teaching: A person plays child, lover, pauper and rich man, each for a moment, and then, made up with wrinkles like an actor, exits behind the curtain of Death.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Calls the actor comparison very impressive: as an actor retires behind the curtain after many parts, so a man, after many roles on the world's stage, retires behind the seat of Death.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates the exit as going behind the scene that veils the abode of Yama, after the role ends with diseased limbs and a wrinkled body.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely, addressing 'O actor man', who vanishes from the stage when death beckons from the wings.

practical_reading: Used to loosen identification with any one role (rich, poor, young, successful): they are costumes in a short play.
misreadings: Not saying life is fake; it is saying roles are temporary
cautions: Ends with death; moderate for the bereaved
speaks_to: identity crisis after losing a role or status
sudden change of fortune, up or down
not_for: fresh grief
someone in a health crisis

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 51 in GRETIL (3.51) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 24. Vivekananda translated it (verse 51).
translation_note: Our Sanskrit reads 'mānadhanātidūram' (very far apart in honour and wealth), and Madhavananda and Vivekananda translate a great or infinite difference between ascetic and king. Our English says the gap 'is not wide', which follows Telang/Joglekar's variant reading (vocative 'mānada', 'not very far'). Either change the English or print the variant Sanskrit and note it.
context: Opens the section comparing the monk and the king (yati-nṛpati-saṃvāda). An ascetic speaks to a king as an equal or better; the next verse sets kingly power over riches against the ascetic's command over words and ideas (52).

key_terms.sense: wisdom gained by serving one's teachers

core_teaching: A learned ascetic tells a king: you have wealth and fame, I have wisdom and a poet's renown; if you turn away from me, I want nothing from you either.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says the sloka is addressed by a monk to a king to show the vanity of his possessions: the king is rich only in wealth, the monk in wisdom, which commands even a king's respect.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'mānada' as a vocative (one who humbles enemies) and translates: the difference between both of us is not at all great; if you are cold to us, we are wholly indifferent to you.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: there is infinite difference between us, so we are not the persons to wait upon kings.

practical_reading: Used to support self-respect before the powerful: learning and integrity are their own wealth, and one need not court approval.
misreadings: Self-respect, not contempt for others or for wealth
Not licence for arrogance toward employers or elders
cautions: Low risk
speaks_to: feeling small before rich or powerful people
scholars, teachers, artists undervalued by the market
not_for: someone whose pride is already isolating them

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 53 in GRETIL (3.53) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 50.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar. GRETIL reads 'sama iha' for our 'sama iva'; same sense.
context: In the monk-and-king dialogue: after the monk's claim of mastery over words (52) and before the verse listing fruits, water, bare ground and bark as enough (54).

key_terms.sense: a difference that makes no difference

core_teaching: Bark or silk, the contentment is the same; the poor one is whoever craves endlessly, and when the mind is content there is no rich or poor.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Adds that one satisfied with even the little he has is as good as rich.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Prefers the silk reading because it contrasts better with bark, and compares Shakespeare's line that the poor but content man is rich enough.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Also prefers the silk reading and finds the 'distinctionless distinction' phrase puzzling, suggesting a sense of greatness for viśeṣa.

practical_reading: A favourite on contentment: redefine poverty as unending craving, so that comparison with richer people loses its sting.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of real material poverty or of fighting it
cautions: Can sound glib to someone in real deprivation
speaks_to: comparison and envy (social media, relatives, colleagues)
financial anxiety that is really about status
not_for: someone facing real hardship (unpaid rent, hunger)

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 57 in GRETIL (3.57) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 23.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar. Madhavananda glosses the fourteen worlds as the whole created universe.
context: In the monk-and-king dialogue, after 'who are we to go to see a king?' (56) and before the verse mocking kings who rejoice over a fragment of an earth that hundreds of rulers have already enjoyed (58).
core_teaching: Great beings have created, ruled, conquered and given away whole worlds like straw; what is this fever of pride in people who rule a few towns?

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the fourteen divisions as the entire created universe, set against pride in ruling a few towns.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Paraphrases the close as asking why people become so infatuated by sovereignty over a few cities; notes the verse is also in the Kāvyasaṅgraha.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains the locative absolute 'when there is lordship over a few towns' and translates the end as a fever of pride or passion.

practical_reading: Used to puncture status pride: any title or position is tiny on the scale of history.
misreadings: Not contempt for leadership or responsibility
cautions: Low risk
speaks_to: a promotion going to one's head
not_for: someone who has just lost a position and feels worthless (may sound like 'it never mattered')

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 62 in GRETIL (3.62) and Madhavananda 1916; in Telang/Joglekar and Wortham it is Vairagya 'Miscellaneous' stanza 24, outside the main hundred.
attribution_note: Part of the Nirnaya Sagar/Chaukhamba vulgate but relegated to the miscellaneous stanzas by Telang and Wortham, so its place in the core collection is less secure.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Wortham (misc. 24): rest, mind; what happens comes about by itself; not dwelling on the past or planning the future, I take the pleasures that come unsought.
context: In the section on stimulating wisdom in the mind (mano-sambodhana), after the verse asking why the heart labours to win other people's favour (61) and before the call to leave the labyrinth of sense objects (63).

key_terms.sense: what happens happens as it does

core_teaching: The mind is told to stop its restless wandering: things unfold as they will, so without brooding on the past or scripting the future, the poet accepts what comes unbidden.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates: rest somewhere; whatever happens in whatever way happens so by itself; not thinking over the past nor resolving about the future, I enjoy what comes without engaging my thoughts.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Says bluntly that the second line is fatalism.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Quotes Kale's alternative: things turn out best when left to their natural course rather than forced by exertion.

practical_reading: Used for the worry loop: once you have done your part, stop rehearsing the past and pre-living the future, and let the next thing arrive.
misreadings: Not an argument against planning or responsibility
Telang calls the second line fatalism; do not present it as a general life philosophy
cautions: Fatalistic ground ('what will be will be') can feel dismissive to someone facing a fixable problem
not_for: someone who needs to act (medical decisions, unsafe situations)
a person in crisis

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 67 in GRETIL (3.67) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 73. Vivekananda translated it (verse 67).
translation_note: Close to Madhavananda. 'Sampāditāḥ praṇayino vibhavaiḥ' is 'what if wealth brings you friends' (Madhavananda) or 'what if suppliants are honoured with grants' (Joglekar); our 'won over friends with your riches' fits the first.
context: In the section on the mind. The preceding verse says enjoy if real pleasure can be found, otherwise plunge into meditation (66); Madhavananda notes that this verse then shows the uselessness of fulfilled desires, and the next (68) names what is worth having: devotion to Shiva, fear of birth and death, solitude, dispassion.

key_terms.sense: an aeon, a day of Brahma

core_teaching: Wealth that grants every wish, victory over enemies, friends won with money, a body lasting an aeon: so what? None of it is the real goal.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Frames the 'so what' as the poet preaching the uselessness of fulfilled worldly desires, since all worldly pleasures are transient and limited.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses kalpa as a day of Brahma, 432 million years, and points to the next stanza for what the poet prefers to all this.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely and joins it to the next verse: the only thing to be desired is renunciation that gives all love to Shiva.

practical_reading: Used to test goals: after each achievement ask 'and then what?' until you reach something that does not need another 'so what'.
misreadings: Read alone it can deepen 'nothing matters'; the tradition reads it with the next verse, which names devotion and dispassion as the answer
cautions: Can feed nihilism or depression if given without verse 68
speaks_to: chasing the next promotion or purchase
not_for: someone depressed or without purpose
a young person just starting to build a life
research_note: Our_note glosses the tradition as 'without knowledge of the self, what then?'. The sources read point to verse 68's answer (devotion to Shiva and renunciation); the self-knowledge gloss is reasonable but not stated there.

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 70 in GRETIL (3.70) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 77. Vivekananda translated it (verse 70).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar. 'Ātmanīna' is 'belonging to the self' (Madhavananda) or 'beneficial to oneself' (Joglekar); a variant reads 'ātma-līna', absorbed in the self. Telang notes Ramarshi takes 'mānasa' as a vocative (O mind), as we do.
context: Our data calls it the closing verse of the section on the mind: after the call to meditate on the infinite Brahman beside which world-sovereignty looks pitiable (69); the next section opens with 'what use are the Vedas...' (71).
core_teaching: The restless mind roams underworld, sky and every direction, yet never, even by accident, turns to the pure Brahman that is its own self and its peace.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains ātmanīna as belonging to the self, since the self's real state is Brahman; the other reading would mean submerged in the self.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Notes Ramarshi takes mānasa as vocative; 'even by mistake' means you not only fail to think of Brahman on purpose, you never stumble on it.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: all this searching is the mind's fickleness; you never remember the Lord within, so how can you be happy?

practical_reading: Used in meditation teaching to name mind-wandering and invite the attention home.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of curiosity or travel
cautions: Low risk
speaks_to: constant searching for the next thing
not_for: someone with ADHD or anxiety who may hear blame for a restless mind

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 71 in GRETIL (3.71) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 81. Vivekananda translated it (verse 71).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda, Joglekar and Vivekananda ('the rest is all shop-keeping').
context: Opens the section discriminating the lasting from the passing (nitya-anitya-vastu-vicāra), after the mind's fruitless roaming (70). The next verse pictures Meru toppling and the seas drying at the end of an age (72).

key_terms.sense: a hut in the village of heaven
the state of bliss in one's own self
the fire at the end of time

core_teaching: Scripture, ritual and learning that only earn a place in heaven are trading; the one thing worth having is entry into the bliss of the self, which burns up worldly sorrow.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says the vast śāstras here mean logic, grammar and the six philosophical systems, vast because of their commentary and argument; heaven is likened to a village of huts.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Calls the rest mere mercenary affairs, except the one way into the place where there is joy in one's self, which destroys worldly misery like the final fire.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Records Ramarshi's gloss of svātmānanda-pada as the seat where there is joy in oneself.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: freedom alone lifts the weight of the world and reveals the Self's blessedness; the rest is shop-keeping.

practical_reading: Used to warn against transactional religion (rituals done to get something) and to point to inner peace as the aim of practice.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of scripture or ritual; a warning against treating them as a transaction
Not anti-learning
cautions: Can offend readers devoted to ritual if not framed
not_for: someone whose ritual practice is their main comfort in grief

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 73 in GRETIL (3.73) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 111 (inside their main Vairagya sequence).
attribution_note: Telang notes it is quoted under another name in the Sharngadhara Paddhati (p. 597); the OCR does not let me read which name.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar (relatives disregard his words, the wife does not nurse him, even the son turns hostile). Wortham reads 'servants cease to obey'.
context: In the section on the lasting and the passing: after the image of Meru falling at the world's end (72) and before the verse on young women fleeing an old man's grey hair (74). Both are portraits of old age.

key_terms.sense: even the son acts like an enemy

core_teaching: A lament on old age: the body fails, and the family stops listening; the wife no longer cares for him and even his son turns hostile.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as a list of bodily decline ending with relatives not valuing one's words, the wife not nursing, and even the son of an aged man turning hostile.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses ādriyate as heeding, śuśrūṣate as serving, and cites a parallel for the line about the hostile son.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders the family lines as servants ceasing to obey, the wife not submissive and the son an enemy.

practical_reading: Our misuse note reads it as a call to keep listening to the old; teachers use it to awaken compassion for ageing parents and to prepare for one's own old age.
misreadings: A lament, not a prediction of every family's future
Not permission to neglect elders
cautions: Graphic bodily decline (drooling, deafness, blindness); painful for those caring for ageing parents or ageing themselves
Family-conflict theme

not_for: elderly readers feeling neglected (may confirm their fear)
someone estranged from a parent or child

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 75 in GRETIL (3.75) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 88. Vivekananda translated it (verse 75).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda, Joglekar and Vivekananda. 'Ātma-śreyas' is one's own highest good (Madhavananda: supreme good; Joglekar: welfare of the soul).
context: In the section on the lasting and the passing, after two portraits of old age (73-74) and before the poet's indecision about how to spend a life of a few blinks (76).

key_terms.sense: digging a well when the house is already on fire

core_teaching: While the body is healthy, old age far off and the senses strong, make a great effort for your highest good; once the house is burning, it is too late to dig a well.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as a call for mighty exertion for one's supreme good while health, senses and life last, for digging a well once the house is on fire avails nothing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the words and quotes Telang that the closing question is an idiom like the English 'what shall we say to such a thing'.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely with urgency: now, now, struggle on, rendering great help to yourself; no use digging a well in a burning house.

practical_reading: One of the most usable verses for younger readers: do the inner work (practice, character, relationships) now, while you have energy, not after a crisis.
misreadings: Not saying it is ever too late to begin; it is about not postponing
cautions: For someone already ill or old, 'too late' can sting
speaks_to: young and middle-aged readers postponing what matters
starting a spiritual or health practice
not_for: someone newly diagnosed or elderly who may hear 'you missed your chance'

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 76 in GRETIL (3.76) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 40.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar. Telang reads living by the Ganges as equivalent to leaving the world, and prefers taking the scripture and poetry options separately.
context: In the section on the lasting and the passing, right after 'dig the well before the house burns' (75). Having urged effort, the poet admits he does not know which path to choose.

key_terms.sense: we do not know what to do

core_teaching: Ascetic retreat, devoted family life, deep study or poetry? With a life that lasts a few blinks, the poet confesses he does not know which to choose.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates: since man's life lasts a few twinklings of the eye, we do not know which of these to undertake.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Notes some take the scripture and poetry phrases as one item but finds it happier to take them separately; renders the close 'we do not know what to do'.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Says resorting to the Ganges stands for leaving the world, and discusses Ramarshi's long gloss, preferring to take the options separately.

practical_reading: A rare honest verse about indecision; teachers use it to name the paralysis of too many good paths, before choosing one.
misreadings: Not a claim that all paths are equal or pointless; the indecision is left unresolved
cautions: Low risk; may mirror anxiety for an indecisive reader
speaks_to: choosing between spiritual life and family duties
not_for: someone already paralysed by indecision who needs a clear step

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 84 in GRETIL (3.84) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 99. Vivekananda translated it (verse 84).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda, Joglekar and Vivekananda. Janārdana is Vishnu (Madhavananda: slayer of the demon Jana).
context: In the section on the worship of Shiva. Madhavananda explains that the previous verse names Shiva as the only refuge, so this verse removes a doubt: the poet does not set Shiva above Vishnu in essence; his love is simply turned to Shiva.

key_terms.sense: the inner self of the universe
he who wears the young moon on his head (Shiva)

core_teaching: Shiva and Vishnu are not different in essence; still, the poet's heart is given to Shiva: one truth, one chosen form of love.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Calls this ishta-nishtha, devotion to one's own ideal: no real difference between Shiva and Vishnu, but the poet is by nature attached to Shiva; lists four senses of 'inner self of the universe'.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Glosses vastu-bheda-pratipatti as a belief in difference and compares a Gita construction for the grammar.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: in Shiva or Vishnu I see no difference, but my love is for Him with the young moon on His forehead.

practical_reading: Used to model devotion without sectarianism: love your chosen form of the divine wholeheartedly without denying others.
misreadings: Not a ranking of Shiva over Vishnu
Not religious relativism that makes devotion pointless
cautions: Low risk; sectarian readers may bristle
speaks_to: devotees who feel torn between deities
not_for: readers outside Hindu devotion without context

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 92 in GRETIL (3.92) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 83. Vivekananda translated it (verse 92).
translation_note: 'Maṇḍalī-mātra' is 'a mere ring/circle' (ours, Vivekananda's 'a little circle'); Madhavananda translates 'a mere reflection', reading the universe as an image in pure consciousness. Joglekar: a mere collection of worlds. Manasvin is the self-controlled, high-minded person.
context: In the section on the way of life of a free ascetic (avadhūta-caryā), after the verse that a worn loincloth, begged food and a calm mind outweigh rule over three worlds (91), and before the poet's farewell to Lakshmi, goddess of wealth (93).

key_terms.sense: the flick of a small fish

core_teaching: To a great mind the whole universe is a small thing and cannot stir greed, just as a small fish's flick cannot churn the ocean.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains: as a fish cannot set the ocean swaying, the universe, a mere image in pure consciousness, cannot move the wise, who are one with that consciousness, to covetousness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Translates: what is a mere collection of worlds to tempt one whose mind is under control? Is the ocean ever agitated by a small fish's gambols?

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: this universe is only a little circle; what is there to desire in it?

practical_reading: Our line widens it from greed to not being shaken by small things, which the ocean image supports: a deep mind is not stirred by petty provocations.
misreadings: Not contempt for the world or for small people
cautions: Low risk
speaks_to: being thrown by small annoyances or criticism
not_for: someone whose distress is serious (it can minimise real pain as a 'small fish')

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 94 in GRETIL (3.94) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 79. Vivekananda translated it (verse 94).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Vivekananda. Wortham reads 'bhuja-latā' as arms of creepers rather than the sage's own arm.
context: In the section on the free ascetic, after the farewell to Lakshmi (93) and before the portrait of the real ascetic living on alms, unattached, clothed in rags (95).

key_terms.sense: the earth as a great bed

core_teaching: The sage sleeps like a king: earth for a bed, his arm for a pillow, the sky a canopy, the breeze a fan, the autumn moon a lamp, and Renunciation as his bride.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates the sage as lying down happily and peacefully, rejoicing in abnegation as his wife, like a monarch of undiminished glory.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Renders: though he has renounced all desires, the sage stretches out like a monarch, delighting in renunciation as his woman.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely, ending: what king is there who can sleep like me in pleasure?

practical_reading: Used to celebrate simplicity: contentment turns the simplest surroundings into a palace.
misreadings: Not romanticising homelessness or poverty
cautions: Could feel glib to someone without a home
not_for: someone facing homelessness or insecure housing

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 96 in GRETIL (3.96) and Madhavananda 1916; Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 56.
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar.
context: In the section on the free ascetic, after the portrait of the real ascetic in rags (95) and before the verse that the Creator provides air for snakes and grass for beasts, so a livelihood exists for the self-devoted too (97).

key_terms.sense: an outcaste, below the four varnas
a mind skilled in discerning reality

core_teaching: People speculate loudly about who the wandering yogi is, outcaste, brahmin, labourer, ascetic or great sage; the yogis walk on, neither angry nor flattered.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains the social labels for the reader: the caṇḍāla is beyond the four castes, the śūdra is the fourth, the twice-born are the first three; the yogis go their way neither pleased nor displeased.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the yogi as one whose intellect is keen at separating reality from appearance, and the crowd as garrulous with doubts; translates that ascetics are neither irritated nor pleased.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders the guesses as questions put directly to the wanderer ('Are you a Chandala?'), sharpening the scene.

practical_reading: Used to steady people who are constantly labelled or judged: let others argue about who you are and keep walking.
misreadings: The verse sets caste labels aside as other people's chatter; it does not endorse them
cautions: Names caste categories, including an outcaste term; explain rather than repeat them
speaks_to: being judged, gossiped about or misjudged
not_for: readers hurt by caste discrimination, unless the labels are carefully framed
research_note: Our verified_with cites 'Vivekananda, Complete Works (see notes)' for this verse; it is not among the verses in Vivekananda's Bhartrihari translation (CW vol. 9), and I did not find another Vivekananda use of it.

verified_ref: Vairagyashataka 100 in GRETIL (3.100) and Madhavananda 1916 (the closing verse); Telang/Joglekar and Wortham 87. Vivekananda translated it (verse 100).
translation_note: Matches Madhavananda and Joglekar ('I now merge in the supreme Brahman'). Teja is fire or light (Joglekar: light). Vivekananda calls water 'sweetheart' where others have 'good kinsman'.
context: The last verse of the Vairagyashataka in Madhavananda's (Nirnaya Sagar) order: after the yogi's longing for Himalayan samādhi with antelopes rubbing against him (98) and the plea to Shiva (99), the knower says goodbye to the five elements that made up his body.

key_terms.sense: a last salutation with folded hands
I dissolve into the supreme Brahman

core_teaching: At the end, the knower thanks earth, wind, fire, water and sky as family: through their company he gained merit and the clear knowledge that dispelled delusion, and now he merges into Brahman.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says the endearing terms suit the blissful parting of a yogin who has passed through the subtle essences of the five elements in the stages of yogic practice.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Reads the sage as saying the elements nursed and helped him, since knowledge of Brahman is impossible without a body made of them; he takes leave with grateful recollection.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: take my last salutation; today I melt into Brahman, my heart purified and delusion gone through your good company.

practical_reading: Used as a model of a grateful farewell: thanking the body and the natural world for what they made possible.
misreadings: Not a wish to die; it is the culmination of a realised life
cautions: A farewell at death; moving at end of life or a funeral, but avoid for anyone expressing a wish to die
Rebirth/merging doctrine may not console every mourner
speaks_to: gratitude for the body and nature
not_for: anyone with suicidal thoughts
fresh, raw grief where 'merging into Brahman' may sound dismissive
